content.overview: Sections 10–12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 form the core statutory gateway for enforceability and capacity. Section 10 identifies the conditions subject to which agreements become contracts; sections 11 and 12 regulate competence and soundness of mind.
content.glance: Sections 10–12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 form the core statutory gateway for enforceability and capacity. Section 10 identifies the conditions subject to which agreements become contracts; sections 11 and 12 regulate competence and soundness of mind.

sections.heading: Section 10 — When agreements become contracts
sections.body: Section 10 states the general rule that agreements are contracts when made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not expressly declared void. The provision remains subject to other provisions of the Act and other laws that Parliament has not displaced.

sections.heading: Section 11 — Competency to contract
sections.body: A person is competent to contract when the person has attained the age of majority according to the law applicable to that person, is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which the person is subject. Competence is therefore a cumulative statutory inquiry.

sections.heading: Section 12 — Sound mind for contracting
sections.body: Section 12 asks whether, at the time of making the contract, the person is capable of understanding the contract and forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon that person’s interests. The section also recognises that a person ordinarily of unsound mind may contract during a lucid interval and that a person ordinarily of sound mind may be incapable of contracting while affected by a condition preventing the statutory capacity.

sections.heading: Sequential application
sections.body: Start with agreement, then test the section 10 requirements. Capacity is not a substitute for free consent, and soundness of mind is only one component of competence. A conclusion on validity should identify the exact statutory defect rather than collapsing all defects into a general statement that the contract is invalid.

sections.heading: Proof and factual assessment
sections.body: Capacity disputes are fact-sensitive. The relevant question under section 12 concerns the person’s condition at the time of contracting and the ability to understand the transaction and form a rational judgment as to its effect. Evidence must therefore be directed to the relevant time and transaction, not merely to a general diagnosis or later condition.

examples.title: Illustration — Section 10 satisfied on the stated facts
examples.body: Two parties of full capacity freely consent to an agreement supported by lawful consideration and a lawful object, and no provision of the Act expressly declares the arrangement void. Section 10 supplies the general statutory basis for treating the agreement as a contract, subject to other applicable law.

examples.title: Boundary case — Capacity must exist at the relevant time
examples.body: A person ordinarily capable of contracting enters a transaction while a condition prevents the person from understanding the transaction or forming a rational judgment about its effect. Section 12 requires the court to assess capacity at the time of contracting rather than relying only on the person’s ordinary condition.

hypotheticals.question: A person is generally of sound mind but, at the time of signing a contract, cannot understand its terms or form a rational judgment about its effect. What is the statutory inquiry?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 12 directs attention to the person’s capacity at the time of making the contract. The question is whether the person could understand the contract and form a rational judgment as to its effect upon the person’s interests.

hypotheticals.question: A party is competent by age and mental capacity but the agreement has an unlawful object. Can section 10 nevertheless treat it as a contract?
hypotheticals.analysis: No conclusion can be reached from capacity alone. Section 10 requires lawful consideration and lawful object in addition to free consent and competency, and it is subject to the other statutory provisions governing enforceability.

rows.left: Cumulative statutory capacity: majority, sound mind and absence of legal disqualification.
rows.right: Specific inquiry into ability to understand the contract and form a rational judgment as to its effect.

rows.left: Competence is a statutory status subject to the conditions in section 11.
rows.right: Capacity is assessed at the time the contract is made.

rows.left: Existence of the promise structure under section 2(e).
rows.right: Agreement satisfying section 10 and the applicable enforceability rules.

rows.left: May exist even though it is not enforceable.
rows.right: Requires the statutory conditions for enforceability.

misconceptions.trap: Treating section 10 as a complete code that ignores every other statutory rule.
misconceptions.correction: Section 10 itself is expressly subject to other provisions of the Act and applicable law.

misconceptions.trap: Equating a general mental-health condition with incapacity under section 12.
misconceptions.correction: The statutory test is functional and transaction-specific: ability to understand the contract and form a rational judgment as to its effect at the time of contracting.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What must be established under sections 10–12?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: The analysis begins with section 10 and asks whether the agreement was made with free consent by competent parties, for lawful consideration and a lawful object, without an applicable statutory declaration of voidness. Sections 11 and 12 then supply the capacity and soundness-of-mind tests.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The provisions should be applied cumulatively and in sequence.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a capacity objection be framed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: The objection should identify the section 11 component said to be absent and, where mental capacity is disputed, apply section 12 to the party’s actual ability at the time of contracting to understand the transaction and form a rational judgment as to its effect.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The submission should be tied to the statutory test rather than a conclusory medical label.

examTips: State section 10 first, then isolate the specific defect.
For capacity disputes, analyse section 11 and section 12 separately.
Use the time-of-contracting test under section 12 rather than a general label.
Address the statutory exceptions and other applicable provisions before concluding.
revisionPoints: Section 10: free consent + competency + lawful consideration + lawful object + no express statutory voidness, subject to other applicable law.
Section 11: majority + sound mind + no legal disqualification.
Section 12: understand the contract + rational judgment about its effect at the time of contracting.
Capacity, consent, legality and voidness are distinct analytical inquiries.
illustrations: Two competent adults freely agree to sell a lawful item for an agreed price; the section 10 conditions are satisfied unless another statutory rule makes the agreement void.

enhancement.definition: Section 10 identifies when agreements become contracts subject to the Act’s conditions; sections 11–12 define competency and soundness of mind.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Enforceability under section 10 depends on multiple cumulative statutory conditions. Competence is separately defined by section 11, while section 12 supplies a functional, time-specific test for soundness of mind.
statutoryFramework: Section 12 — sound mind and the relevant-time functional test.
essentialIngredients: Test lawful consideration and lawful object.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 10 is not merely a definition of a contract; it states the conditions under which agreements become contracts, while expressly preserving the operation of other provisions of the Act and other laws. Section 11 makes competence cumulative: majority, sound mind and absence of legal disqualification. Section 12 refines the mental-capacity inquiry by asking whether the person could understand the contract and form a rational judgment as to its effect upon the person’s interests at the relevant time. This structure prevents a court from substituting a general conclusion about age or mental condition for the statutory test.
examples: Two parties of full capacity freely consent to an agreement supported by lawful consideration and a lawful object, and no provision of the Act expressly declares the arrangement void.
